parts.article:
Antarctic research
 
Thirteen nations took part in the recent International Polar Year
 
(A) New Zealand’s contribution to International Polar Year was a 52-day voyage by the ship Tangaroa in order to conduct research in Antarctica’s Ross Sea. Lead scientist Mary Livingston emphasises just what a multi-faceted expedition this was, bringing together zoologists, oceanographers, meteorologists and other scientists from the Ministry of Fisheries, the National Institute for Water and Atmospheric Research, the National Museum and various universities, to study life beneath the seas of Antarctica. Competition for berths – the ship can carry 44 people, including 13 crew – was fierce. Voyage leader Stu Hanchet says, ‘We could have filled the science positions four times over … we had so many people requesting a berth … We ended up with a really strong team.’
 
(B) It would be hard to overstate how hostile the Antarctic environment is for scientists. The Tangaroa’s captain, Graham Leachman, explains that the Ross Sea is subject to katabatic winds* that sweep down off the Antarctic continent to create rough seas. Another danger is the possibility of the ship colliding with floating ice. ‘Even though the ship’s officers use all sorts of high-tech equipment … none of it can tell you how thick the ice is,’ says Leachman, ‘and you still can’t beat looking out of the window.’ In the dark, he says, you can’t tell how thick the ice is, but if you can see its colour, it’s possible to estimate. This is why he prefers sailing in summer, when the hours of daylight in these high latitudes are longest, even though this plays tricks with his passengers’ body clocks.
 
(C) Analysis of what the expedition found continues, but it’s likely that several new species have been discovered and numerous other secrets revealed about life 3,000 metres below the surface. ‘We have collected huge worms and strange crustaceans,’ says Livingston, ‘but most impressive of all were the starfish that measured more than half a metre across – that’s most abnormal for creatures belonging to this species.’ This phenomenon of Antarctic seas is called ‘gigantism’ – the fact that some species grow to unusually large sizes. Livingston suggests various possible causes for gigantism, including the extreme cold, few predators and high levels of oxygen in the seawater, but as yet, no final determination can be made. Another interesting discovery was that in some places every inch of the sea floor was covered with life, whereas elsewhere icebergs have scoured out deep scars and ravines in the sea floor as they go by.
 
(D) By using deep-sea trawl nets, high-definition cameras and water samplers, the team has revealed that many of the creatures that live at extreme depths have a bizarre appearance. Among them were spotted tunicates, plankton-eating animals that are slender structures that appear to be fashioned from glass. The most fearsome-looking fish was the Southern Ocean daggertooth, a species that is ‘monocyclic’, meaning the fish die after the first spawning. They are also unusual for being capable of shedding their teeth and growing a new set. Another predatory fish brought to the surface was the stareater, an extraordinary species that has an appendage like a piece of cord hanging from its chin. In these deep, dark waters, this glows red and attracts prey to swim within striking distance. Just as impressive and much more beautiful were the basket stars, a species related to starfish that lives on the seabed. The basket stars’ five arms branch out numerous times to form a spectacular fan-like structure which they turn to face into the current so that food is brought into their embrace.
 
(E) But whatever exciting discoveries were made, everyday life onboard ship in the Ross Sea is unrelenting. Most people share a cabin with one other person – they’re allocated so that as one person begins their 12 hours off duty, the other occupant is starting work on deck. The fresh food runs out in a few days and after that, most provisions are frozen, canned or dried. Expedition general manager Fred Smits recognises that the cook has an essential role in ensuring the well-being of those onboard. ‘When you are at sea for so long,’ he says, ‘you think a lot about your next meal.’
 
(F) Perhaps most controversially, one of the precious berths on the Tangaroa was taken up by cameraman Max Quinn, who filmed a documentary about the voyage. Quinn’s inclusion wasn’t welcomed at first. ‘Scientists by nature,’ Livingston says, ‘tend to be camera-shy and quiet. They’re not into having cameras there, so it was difficult getting everyone’s permission and agreement.’ But in the end Quinn fitted in very well. ‘The trick,’ he says, ‘is to mostly film the scientists at work, in their professional roles … rather than eating their breakfast.’ He knows when not to intrude. The documentary is a window on a trip few people get to make and also a peek into what research really looks like. ‘Science,’ says Livingston, ‘is intrepid, more so than people realise. It’s not necessarily examining dry samples in the laboratory, but can also mean braving the elements on deck. That’s what the documentary captures, the sense of real people with real lives.’
*Katabatic wind: a wind caused by the local downward motion of cool air.

analyses.content: 只有D段具体列出了科研工具清单，其他段落虽然提到high-tech equipment（B段），但没有给出具体细节。
(Paragraph D) “By using deep-sea trawl nets, high-definition cameras and water samplers, the team has revealed...”
题目提到科学家所用一些设备的细节。D段开头列举了“deep-sea trawl nets（深海拖网）”、“high-definition cameras（高清摄像机）”和“water samplers（取水器）”，完全对应“details of some equipment”，选 D。

questions.question: a description of the challenging sailing conditions in Antarctica

analyses.content: 题目提到对南极艰难航行条件的描述。B段详细描述了“katabatic winds（下降风）”造成的巨浪、船只可能与“floating ice（浮冰）”相撞的危险以及在黑暗中无法判断冰层厚度的困难，选 B。
“Challenging sailing conditions” 对应原文的 “hostile environment”、“winds”、“danger” 和 “thick the ice is”。
(Paragraph B) “...the Ross Sea is subject to katabatic winds... Another danger is the possibility of the ship colliding with floating ice.”

questions.question: information about the composition of the scientific group

analyses.content: 题目提到关于科学团队构成的信息。A段列举了此次探险集合了“zoologists（动物学家）”、“oceanographers（海洋学家）”、“meteorologists（气象学家）”以及来自不同机构的科学家，这就是团队的构成，选 A。
“Composition of the scientific group” 对应原文列举的一长串职业名词。
(Paragraph A) “...bringing together zoologists, oceanographers, meteorologists and other scientists from...”

questions.question: the identity of a potentially unpopular person on the ship

analyses.content: “Potentially unpopular person” 对应原文的 “wasn't welcomed at first”。
题目提到船上一个可能不受欢迎的人的身份。F段提到摄影师 Max Quinn 占据了一个宝贵的床位，且最初“Quinn’s inclusion wasn’t welcomed（奎因的加入不受欢迎）”，选 F。
(Paragraph F) “...berths... was taken up by cameraman Max Quinn... Quinn’s inclusion wasn’t welcomed at first.”

groups.contentHtml:
The expedition’s findings
Analysis continues of the expedition’s remarkable discoveries, including a , very notable for its unusual width. The reasons why creatures grow so large at great depths in Antarctica may include the highly oxygenated water, the temperature, or the small number of . A further fascinating finding was the existence of canyons in the seabed caused by passing . Many creatures living at great depth look very strange, such as tunicates, which seem to be made of . One frightening-looking fish species is characterised by the loss of its and the fact that it spawns only once. Another fish has something like a length of string attached to its that assists with hunting.

analyses.content: 题目说发现包括一种因其不寻常的宽度而非常引人注目的____。原文C段提到最令人印象深刻的是测量直径超过半米的“starfish（海星）”，填 starfish。
“Unusual width” 对应原文的 “measured more than half a metre across”。
(Paragraph C) “...but most impressive of all were the starfish that measured more than half a metre across...”
题目说生物长得巨大的原因可能包括高含氧量的水、温度或少量的____。原文C段提到巨大化的可能原因包括极寒、高氧以及“few predators（很少的捕食者）”，填 predators。
“Small number of” 是 “few” 的同义替换。
(Paragraph C) “Livingston suggests various possible causes... including the extreme cold, few predators and high levels of oxygen...”
(Paragraph C) “...icebergs have scoured out deep scars and ravines in the sea floor as they go by.”
“Caused by passing...” 对应原文的 “scoured out... as they go by”。
题目说海底峡谷是由经过的____造成的。原文C段末尾说“icebergs（冰山）”在经过时在海底刮出了深深的伤痕和峡谷，填 icebergs。
题目说被囊类动物（tunicates）看起来像是由____制成的。原文D段说它们看起来像是“fashioned from glass（由玻璃制成）”，填 glass。
“Made of” 是 “fashioned from” 的同义替换。
(Paragraph D) “...tunicates... appear to be fashioned from glass.”
题目说一种可怕的鱼的特征是失去它的____并且只产卵一次。原文D段提到 Southern Ocean daggertooth 会“shedding their teeth（脱落牙齿）”并长出新的，填 teeth。
“Loss of” 对应原文的 “shedding”。
(Paragraph D) “They are also unusual for being capable of shedding their teeth...”
(Paragraph D) “...has an appendage like a piece of cord hanging from its chin.”
题目说另一种鱼在其____上连接着像绳子一样的东西来辅助捕猎。原文D段提到 stareater 有一个附属物像绳子一样挂在它的“chin（下巴）”上，填 chin。
题目是介词 to，原文是 hanging from，描述的是同一个身体部位。

analyses.content: 题目匹配观点 F (The nature of scientific work may surprise some people)。原文F段末尾引用 Livingston 的话：“Science is intrepid, more so than people realise.（科学是无畏的，比人们意识到的更甚。）” 这意味着人们可能对科学工作的本质感到惊讶，选 F。
“Surprise some people” 对应 “more so than people realise”。
(Paragraph F) “‘Science,’ says Livingston, ‘is intrepid, more so than people realise.’”
题目匹配观点 G (More applications to join the group were received than there were places)。原文A段 Hanchet 说：“We could have filled the science positions four times over...（我们可以把科学职位填满四次……）”，说明申请人数远超名额，选 G。
“Filled... four times over” 形象地表达了供不应求（more applications than places）。
(Paragraph A) “Voyage leader Stu Hanchet says, ‘We could have filled the science positions four times over...’”
题目匹配观点 B (Respecting your subjects’ privacy gets the best results)。原文F段 Quinn 说诀窍是主要拍摄科学家工作时而非吃早餐时，他知道“when not to intrude（何时不该打扰）”，即尊重隐私，选 B。
“Not to intrude” 和 “rather than eating their breakfast” 都是尊重隐私（privacy）的具体表现。
(Paragraph F) “...Max Quinn... ‘The trick,’ he says, ‘is to mostly film the scientists at work... He knows when not to intrude.’”
